docs.title: 🧠 EEG Data Acquisition Protocol
docs.text: This protocol outlines the standard operating procedure for preparing a participant and acquiring clean EEG data in the Murali Lab.

docs.title: 📋 Pre-Session Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Workstation turned on and impedance check software running.
  • [ ] EEG cap size selected based on participant's head circumference.
  • [ ] Adequate supply of conductive gel and clean syringes.
  • [ ] Sanitized cotton swabs and alcohol prep pads ready.

docs.title: 1. Participant Preparation
docs.text:
1. Measure the participant's head circumference from the nasion to the inion to verify cap size.
  2. Mark the Cz position using an erasable skin marker.
  3. Clean the skin at electrode site locations using an alcohol prep pad to lower skin impedance.

Pro Tip

Ensure the participant's hair is completely dry before applying the cap. Wet hair can cause electrical bridging between neighboring channels!

docs.title: 2. Cap Application & Gel Injection
docs.text:
• Place the cap on the participant's head, aligning Cz with your marked spot.
  • Secure the chin strap comfortably.
  • Use a blunt-tip syringe to push aside hair and inject a small amount of conductive gel into each electrode well.

Safety Warning

Never press too hard with the blunt-tip syringe. It should never cause pain or scratch the participant's skin.

docs.title: 🧪 Lab Protocols & Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs)
docs.text:
Welcome to the Murali Lab Protocol Repository. This section serves as the centralized directory for all experimental workflows, data analysis pipelines, and equipment operation guidelines used in our laboratory.

Mandatory Onboarding Check

All lab members and research assistants must review the relevant safety and hardware protocols before conducting experiments with human participants or lab equipment.

docs.title: EEG Preprocessing
docs.text: (Note: These whole preprocessing steps are for reference purposes only. Please verify the complete preprocessing steps with Prof. Vignesh before implementing.)

docs.title: 1. Purpose and Pre-Processing Philosophy
docs.text:
Preprocessing has two objectives: data transformation (converting raw data into a computable, analyzable format) and artifact handling (removing or attenuating non-neural contamination, such as eye movements, muscle activity, and electrical noise).

There is no single universal pipeline. Steps should be selected based on

  1. Data quality/noise level
  2. The intended analysis (ERP vs. oscillatory vs. connectivity vs. BCI classification)
  3. Requirements of downstream algorithms (e.g., ICA needs high-pass filtering first)
  4. Comparability with prior literature.

Document every parameter used at every step - this is required for reproducibility per the OHBM COBIDAS-MEEG reporting guidelines (Pernet et al., 2020, Nature Neuroscience) and the Keil et al. (2014) EEG/MEG publication guidelines committee report.

Note the ongoing debate: Delorme (2023, Scientific Reports, "EEG is better left alone") argues excessive preprocessing can be unnecessary or harmful for very clean data, while de Cheveigné (2023) and Larsen & Versace (2024) counter that preprocessing remains essential for noisier/complex datasets (e.g., mobile EEG, motor imagery paradigms with muscle/movement contamination).

docs.title: 2. Pre-Preprocessing: Data Quality at Acquisition (Prevention)
docs.text:
Preprocessing quality is capped by acquisition quality. Before touching the data:

  • [ ] Confirm channel montage/coordinates were imported correctly;
  • [ ] Electrode position accuracy matters for interpolation, referencing, and source work
  • [ ] Keep electrode impedances low - below 10 kΩ for passive electrodes; active electrodes can tolerate >20 kΩ without quality loss (Kappenman & Luck, 2010, Psychophysiology).
  • [ ] Log all sources of technical artifact during the session (line noise, cable movement, static discharge, electrode pops), since these inform later cleaning decisions.
  • [ ] For mobile/motor tasks (walking, cycling, motor imagery with limb movement), expect rhythmic motion artifacts synchronized to movement frequency - plan extra EMG/movement channels or accelerometry if possible.

docs.title: Step 1: Initial Data Inspection
docs.text:
• Verify all channels/coordinates loaded correctly; check for flat or non-functioning channels and mislabeled/missing event markers.
  • Standardise/rename event markers for consistency; discard channels/segments irrelevant to analysis.

docs.title: Step 2: Resampling (if needed)
docs.text:
• Downsample high acquisition rates (e.g., 1000 Hz) to reduce file size/computation. For analyses up to the Beta band (\~30 Hz), 250–500 Hz is typically sufficient; EMG, fMRI-gradient, or TMS-pulse correction require higher rates first, then downsample afterwards.
  • Always low-pass filter before downsampling to prevent aliasing — many toolboxes do this automatically, but verify.

docs.title: Step 3: Filtering
docs.text:
• Apply non-causal, zero-phase filters (preserves phase of retained frequencies):
  • High-pass: 0.1–0.5 Hz to remove slow drifts (body sway, skin potentials).
  • Low-pass: \~45 Hz cutoff for typical cognitive/oscillatory EEG (removes muscle/high-frequency noise); adjust upward if gamma-band or EMG content is of interest.
  • Notch filter: 50 or 60 Hz (per your region's mains frequency) plus harmonics, for line noise.
  • Choose FIR or IIR based on your needs; higher filter order \= steeper roll-off but reduced temporal precision. Use the half-power (−3 dB) or half-amplitude (−6 dB) cutoff convention consistently and report which one you used.
  • Filter minimally and only as needed - filtering can distort data in non-obvious ways (de Cheveigné & Nelken, 2019, Neuron; Widmann et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2024).

docs.title: Step 4: Bad Channel Detection and Interpolation
docs.text:
• Identify flat, noisy, or persistently artifactual channels using visual inspection or automated metrics (e.g., within the PREP pipeline; Bigdely-Shamlo et al., 2015, Front. Neuroinform.).
  • Interpolate using spherical spline interpolation (standard default in most toolboxes). Use sparingly - over-interpolation can distort true brain activity; there's no fixed cap, but keep it minimal and report the count/percentage interpolated.
  • Order matters: interpolate bad channels before applying an average reference to preserve balanced spatial sampling; also, running ICA before interpolation/re-referencing avoids rank-deficiency problems.

docs.title: Step 5: Re-referencing
docs.text:
• Choose a reference scheme deliberately: online reference proximity can suppress amplitude near that site; use of Average Reference improves SNR but requires ≥64 channels with even scalp coverage and no remaining bad channels (Bigdely-Shamlo et al., 2015; Hu et al., 2018, J Neural Eng; Tsuchimoto et al., 2021, J Neurosci Methods).
  • For mastoid-referenced setups, average the left/right mastoids to avoid hemispheric bias.
  • Match your reference scheme to the literature you intend to compare against.

docs.title: Step 6: Independent Component Analysis (ICA) for Stereotyped Artifacts
docs.text: Used to correct eye blinks, eye movements, and muscle activity (spatially/temporally consistent artifacts) without discarding data points.

docs.title: Algorithm options:
docs.text:
• Infomax ICA (Makeig et al., 1996) — most widely used; FastICA (Hyvärinen & Oja, 2000);
  • RELICA (Artoni et al., 2014);
  • AMICA (Palmer et al., 2010; Klug et al., 2024).

Algorithm choice depends on your data's artifact profile (Delorme et al., 2012; Klug et al., 2024).

docs.title: Requirements for good ICA decomposition:
docs.text:
• Use ≥64 channels where possible for adequate spatial resolution (Cohen, 2014; Klug & Gramann, 2020, Eur J Neurosci).
  • Sufficient training data: at least (channels² × 20) data points for \<64 channels, or (channels² × 30) for ≥64 channels (Makeig & Onton, 2011).
  • Apply a high-pass filter (\~1–2 Hz) beforehand to remove slow drifts that degrade decomposition quality; you can later apply ICA weights to a less-filtered copy of the data to avoid distorting ERP timing (Debener et al., 2010; Klug & Gramann, 2020; Winkler et al., 2015).
  • Run ICA before interpolation or average referencing to avoid rank-deficiency (reduced effective number of independent channels), or reduce the number of extracted components accordingly.

docs.title: Component classification:
docs.text:
Visually inspect the topography, time course, and spectrum of each component. Automated classifiers such as ICLabel (Pion-Tonachini et al., 2019, NeuroImage) assign each independent component a probability across seven classes - Brain, Muscle, Eye, Heart, Line Noise, Channel Noise, Other - and are available in EEGLAB (MATLAB) and via mne-icalabel (Python).

ICLabel expects extended-Infomax ICA on average-referenced data filtered \~1–100 Hz.

Avoid over-correction: only remove components confidently identified as artifact; removing components containing genuine brain signal degrades data quality.

docs.title: Step 7: Regression-Based Ocular Correction (Alternative/Supplement to ICA)
docs.text: The Gratton & Coles (1983) algorithm regresses out blink/eye-movement contributions using EOG channels — computationally cheap but requires good EOG recordings (Jiang et al., 2019, Sensors, review of EEG artifact removal methods).

docs.title: Step 8: Rejection of Non-Stereotyped Artifacts
docs.text:
For sporadic events (electrode pops, gross movement, transient muscle tension) that don't have a consistent spatial signature suitable for ICA correction:

  • Detect via automatic thresholding (amplitude, kurtosis, joint probability) or manual visual marking. No universal threshold exists - tune to your dataset and apply consistently across subjects, adjusting only when a dataset is clearly noisier.
  • Reject affected trials/channels/segments, or in extreme cases, the entire session.
  • Best practice: combine correction (ICA/regression) with rejection rather than relying on either alone, especially for mobile/motor paradigms (Zhang et al., 2024; Gorjan et al., 2022)

docs.title: Step 9: Segmentation (Epoching)
docs.text:
• Define pre- and post-event windows based on your paradigm and expected neural latency.
  • For time-frequency/wavelet analysis, add safety margins to both segment edges to avoid edge effects and smearing (Herrmann et al., 2014, Brain Topography; Roach & Mathalon, 2008).
  • For FFT/Welch spectral analysis, ensure segment length covers at least one cycle of your lowest frequency of interest; use power-of-two lengths for computational efficiency.
  • For motor imagery/BCI classification, epoch relative to cue onset with sufficient pre-cue baseline for baseline correction and post-cue window covering the full imagined-movement period .

docs.title: 4. Automated Preprocessing Pipelines (Optional, for Standardisation)
docs.text:
If you want a validated, standardised pipeline rather than assembling steps manually:

Pipeline Platform Notes PREP EEGLAB/MATLAB Standardised preprocessing for large-scale EEG (line noise removal, robust referencing, bad channel detection) (Bigdely-Shamlo et al., 2015) HAPPE EEGLAB/MATLAB Designed for developmental/high-artifact data (Gabard-Durnam et al., 2018; updated Monachino et al., 2022) ADJUST EEGLAB/MATLAB Automated IC artifact detection (Mognon et al., 2011) RELAX EEGLAB/MATLAB Automated cleaning pipeline (Bailey et al., 2023) DISCOVER-EEG EEGLAB/MATLAB Fully automated pipeline for biomarker discovery (Gil Ávila et al., 2023, Scientific Data) ICLabel / mne-icalabel EEGLAB or MNE-Python Automated IC classification (Pion-Tonachini et al., 2019)

If you are proficient with MNE-Python and EEGLAB, mne-icalabel + a custom MNE pipeline, or EEGLAB with ICLabel/ADJUST, are both suitable starting points; you can build a hybrid pipeline and script it for batch/version-controlled processing.

docs.title: 5. Special Consideration for Motor Imagery / BCI Pipelines
docs.text:
• A comparative study (Gao et al., 2025, [pipeline effects on motor imagery classification]) found that baseline correction and band-pass filtering consistently provided the most beneficial preprocessing effects for motor-imagery classification accuracy, while more complex steps (ICA, surface Laplacian) had more variable benefit depending on the dataset - worth validating empirically on your own data rather than assuming a heavier pipeline is always better.
  • Surface Laplacian/Current Source Density (CSD) is commonly used as a spatial filter prior to connectivity or sensorimotor rhythm analyses to reduce volume conduction effects.
  • Movement and EMG contamination are more prominent in active motor tasks; apply the movement-artefact-specific guidance in Gorjan et al. (2022) and consider dedicated EMG channels for muscle-artefact regression.

docs.title: 6. Documentation and Reporting Checklist (for Publication/Reproducibility)
docs.text:
• Acquisition system (manufacturer/model), electrode count, montage, electrode type (active/passive, material).
  • Sampling rate, analogue filter bandwidth, and any online notch filtering.
  • Reference and ground electrode locations (both online and any offline re-referencing scheme).
  • All offline filter parameters (type, order, cutoff, causal vs. zero-phase).
  • Bad channel count/criteria and interpolation method.
  • ICA algorithm, number of components removed, and classification method/criteria (manual or ICLabel-based).
  • Artifact rejection thresholds/criteria and percentage of data/trials rejected.
  • Epoching window and baseline correction window.
  • Software and version numbers for every processing step (supports exact reproducibility).

docs.title: BrainVision ActiCHamp
docs.text:
This is the system setup we have in EEG Room 101. We use system 1 to monitor and record EEG data, while system 2 presents stimuli and sends markers to the EEG device. System 2 is mirrored in the participants' seating room.
  1. First step, turn on both systems.
  2. Connect the EEG amplifier with the battery as per the connection shown

  3. Now we’ll connect the EEG electrode set and the ground electrodes. Be very careful while handling these wires, as they are very delicate.

  4. Connect the first electrode set (Green colour, marked 1-32) and the ground electrode as shown in the photo. If you need a 64-channel setup, connect the appropriate electrode set to the next slot. For a 128-channel setup, connect the 4 electrode sets in their respective slots in order.

  5. Complete setup

  6. Now insert this dongle (UR13827) into system 1

  7. Now open BrainVision Recorder

  8. This is the main interface

  1. Click on File, then New Workspace

  2. This pop-up window will open up. Click the Browse button next to Raw File Folder, then select the folder where you want to keep your workspace. Then Click Next

  3. This pop-up window will open next. Click on Scan for Amplifier. It will automatically scan the number of connected electrodes with their labels. Set the sampling rate as per your requirements. Set the reference channel number as required. At the bottom of the pop-up window, you will see a button named Use Electrode Position File. Make sure the proper channel location file (.bvef) has been selected. Then click Next.

  4. This pop-up window will open. If you need to set up filters, you can do so here; otherwise, click Next

  5. This pop-up window will open next. If you want to visualise real-time average segmentation, you can do so here; otherwise, click Next

  6. You will see this window to save your workspace. Name it properly and save

  7. Now you can click on File and select Open Workspace

  8. After selecting your workspace, its name should appear in the bottom right corner

  9. Now click on Impedance check

  10. It will open this interface

  11. You can change the colour limit according to the impedance values (Green for 0-10 KOhm, Yellow to Red for 10-30 KOhm).

  12. Now you can start the capping part.
  13. Make sure that the participant reads the information sheet and signs the consent form.
  14. Measure the head size
  15. Clean the forehead and mastoid properly.
  16. Put the Cap on
  17. First, place the ground electrode, then the remaining electrodes one by one, properly. Handle all electrodes very carefully.
  18. Once you are satisfied with the impedance level of all electrodes, you are ready to record.
  19. Click on the Record button to start recording

docs.title: Check after Recording
docs.text:
Once you have recorded your first data, check the following information

  1. Number of channels recorded
  2. Sampling rate
  3. Channel Labels for the given electrode set
  4. Channel Location
  5. Stimulus Markers Labels
  6. Stimulus Markers Time

docs.title: Murali Lab – Behavioural Experiments Wiki
docs.text:
So, finally, you’re here. Specifically in the behavioural experiment section of the Murali Lab wiki.

Chances are, you’ve just joined the lab and landed on the behavioural side of things. Whether you’re stepping in as project staff, a research intern, or a new PhD scholar, we’re genuinely glad you're here. You have got your workspace set up and someone pointed you to this page.

Running a behavioural study is a long process. It involves a lot of moving parts, from coming up with the initial idea to actually sitting down with a participant and making sense of the data afterward. You know the classic Hebbian rule, neurons that fire together, wire together. Think of this wiki as how we wire together as a team. It’s our shared synaptic space. Every time you read a protocol, ask a question, or troubleshoot a script, you're strengthening our collective network. You don't have to build these pathways alone, we're right here with you to help you get up to speed.

So, let's fire together.

docs.title: Behavioural Experiment Flow
docs.text:
To keep things simple, most of our lab study follows the same basic lifecycle. We will dive into the deep details of each step later on, but here is the standard flow of a behavioural experiment from start to finish:

  1. Problem statement
  2. Drafting the stimuli
  3. Experiment design
  4. Recruitment
  5. Consent form
  6. Participant data collection
  7. Organising the data
  8. Analysis

docs.title: 3.Experiment design
docs.text:
As you know, most experiment problems don’t start in the experiment design software. They start earlier, when the task, stimuli, or trial structure hasn’t been fully nailed down yet. At this stage, we’ll assume you already have:

  1. a clear problem statement or research question
  2. a rough hypothesis or expected behavioural effect
  3. a draft of your stimuli and procedure

If you don’t have all of these yet, that’s completely fine. However, we suggest you try to get them sorted before going too deep into the build. A clear design makes the design part much easier, and it saves you from rewriting half the experiment later.

There are plenty of tools out there for building behavioural tasks : PsychoPy, E-Prime, MATLAB/Psychtoolbox, jsPsych, and a handful of others(see here). In this section, we’re focusing on PsychoPy and it’s what we use for most of our behavioural paradigm.

docs.title: 3.1 Installation PsychoPy
docs.text:
Before you start building, make sure PsychoPy is installed on your system. If you are using a lab machine, it may already be installed. If you need to install it yourself, download the latest stable version from the official PsychoPy website. Unless the PI tells you to use a specific version, always go for the most recent stable release. Once it is installed, open it once just to make sure everything launches properly.

| If you get stuck, don’t worry, just ask someone in the lab. We can help you set it up.

docs.title: 3.2 Intro to PsychoPy
docs.text:
There are two ways to build your experiment in PsychoPy.

1) Builder view (for those not comfortable with programming) : It uses a simple drag-and-drop interface. Instead of writing code, you build your experiment step-by-step. You can easily add things like pictures, instructions, or keyboard responses, and adjust their settings using simple menus. If you ever need a little extra control, you can add tiny bits of code later as well. It’s highly visual, easy to test out your ideas, and honestly where most of us start. You can see what the Builder window looks like in Figure 1 below.

1) Documentation 2) Video Tutorials

    ![][image1]

Fig. 1 PsychoPy Builder view

2) Coder view (for those comfortable with programming): This is where we write the experiment as a full Python script. Instead of dragging and dropping, you build the task directly in code. This gives you much more control over what happens on every single trial. Some people prefer this route, especially when an experiment gets more complex or when you need very specific control. If you are new to coding, don't worry, you can always start in Builder and explore this view later when you feel ready. You can see what the Coder window looks like in Figure 2 below. 1) Documentation 2) Video Tutorial

                             *Fig. 2 PsychoPy Coder view*

When you first open PsychoPy, it will usually open in the Builder view by default. You can easily switch back and forth between Builder and Coder using the View menu (see the Fig. 3). There is also the Runner window(see the Fig. 4), this is where you will actually launch your experiment and keep an eye on outputs or error messages.

Fig. 3 PsychoPy view menu

Fig. 4 PsychoPy Runner window

The important thing to remember is that both routes can produce the same experiment. A task built in Builder and a task written in Coder view can be structurally identical once they run. The trial timing, stimulus order, and response logging do not change just because you chose one over the other. So don’t stress about picking the right one. Start where you’re comfortable, and switch when it makes sense.

docs.title: 3.3 Collecting data: offline or online
docs.text:
PsychoPy also supports two modes of data collection.

Offline means running the experiment on a lab computer, with the participant sitting in front of you, or at least in the same testing environment. This is what we usually use for in-person behavioural sessions because we have control over timing, hardware, and distractions.

Online means exporting the task to run in a browser through platform “Pavlovia”. This is useful when we need larger samples or when in-person testing is not practical. Timing is less precise, but you gain flexibility.

docs.title: 3.3 Into the Lab
docs.text:
When you're ready to design and test your experiments, head over to Room 101. You can use the dedicated lab computer there, specifically System 2 (see Fig. 5 to help you find it).

                         *Fig. 5 Room 101 view*
